articles.title: How the restaurant burger went from cheap indulgence to luxury meal
articles.summary: The $30 burger can be found on menus from New York to California, despite efforts to rein in soaring beef prices.
articles.body:
The Burger Américain, a fastidious and Frenchified version of the Big Mac served at Le Diplomate, set diners back $14 when Stephen Starr debuted his stylish brasserie in Washington in 2013. Thirteen years later, the same burger and fries cost $29.

Starr had a one-word reaction when informed about the 100-percent-plus price increase for one of Washington's favorite burgers :

Recipes, food trends and culinary inspiration. Sign up for free

If Starr, a highly decorated restaurateur with dining rooms in multiple cities, is stunned by the burger inflation at one of his own places, imagine how other Americans feel. The wholesale price of ground beef has soared between 18 and 30 percent in the past few years, restaurateurs tell The Washington Post, and that doesn't take into account the other factors contributing to the increasingly lofty price of a restaurant burger: insurance, labor, rent, utilities, repairs. Prices for each have increased as well, owners say.

A $30 — or higher — burger can be found on menus from New York to California , but operators say these prices reflect the reality of current restaurant economics. "Restaurants are not gouging people," Starr said in an interview. "They are simply responding to their own expenses."

To compound the problem for burger enthusiasts, consumers are seeing similar increases in supermarket ground beef.

The costs are adding up to something that earlier generations once considered unthinkable: The hamburger — a deeply American dish beloved across the socioeconomic spectrum — has become unaffordable to many. It's not just finicky, chef-crafted restaurant burgers, either, the ones built with dry-aged beef or stuffed with foie gras or topped with black truffles. Low-income Americans are scaling back on McDonald's as they struggle to cover the ever-increasing costs of daily life. Some say the revamped McValue Menu offers little to justify the title . Some fast food workers can't even afford the very meals they prepare and sell .

"To me, a hamburger should be an everyday enjoyment that should be affordable, and it should be something that people can comfortably do and not have to break the bank over," said Andrew Schnipper, managing partner of Hamburger America, the celebrated diner in New York City, co-owned by burger scholar George Motz.

Since 2023, restaurant burger prices have increased 14 percent, according to Datassential's Burger Price Index report , last updated in March. The report pulls data from 14 full- and limited-service restaurant chains. The menu increases, while significant, still haven't kept pace with beef production costs, which have skyrocketed nearly 44 percent since 2023, according to a Washington Post analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The data suggest, in other words, that even as Americans complain about overpriced burgers , especially among casual chains, prices could even be worse without some clever cost manipulations by restaurant operators.

Restaurants have developed a number of tricks to try to absorb the rising cost of beef without passing it all on to consumers.

Some rely on a streamlined, high-volume, quick-serve model — with few menu options and an efficient method for preparing burgers fast — to keep prices low. Others, especially full-service restaurants with larger menus, spread the inflated beef costs among other dishes so they're not concentrated in the burger price. Still others look for ways to reduce costs across the entire operation, whether negotiating better deals for paper products or using technology to schedule workers more efficiently. Some may just eat a fraction of those costs, cutting into their own profits.

As the founder and chair of the board for both Shake Shack and Union Square Hospitality Group, Danny Meyer understands how to squeeze out savings in both burger chains and full-service restaurants.

"The last thing one ever wants to do is to pass on costs to the consumer," Meyer said in an interview. "The second-to-last thing people want to do is to lose money, because then you don't have a business. "

Burger lovers aren't finding much relief at the supermarket, either. The cost of preparing a quarter-pounder at home, complete with bun, cheese and toppings, has jumped by 14.5 percent in a two-year span, more than double the rate of inflation for that period, based on a 12-month rolling average of prices. The cheeseburger would cost on average about $2.29, up from $2 two years ago, according to a Post analysis of average retail prices collected by the BLS.

The patty alone accounted for $1.67 of that price. Since 1984, ground beef has become four times as expensive, and it accounts for roughly three-quarters of the total rise in ingredient costs. Everything else on the burger has stayed comparatively cheap.

Beef prices have increased more sharply in the past two years: Ground chuck, the cut most often used for burgers, sold for an average of $6.85 per pound in July, up 25 percent from July 2024.

Beef consumption per person has remained broadly flat for several years, between 55 and 57 pounds a year, though consumption has dropped by more than a third since 1976, when Americans ate 89 pounds annually, according to the Agriculture Department. The flat rate is still notable, given the sharp increase in price, said Andrew Griffith, a professor in the Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics at the University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture.

"The whole point of higher prices is to ration consumption of a product," said Griffith, who runs his own farm about 60 miles southwest of Nashville. "We definitely see that in the marketplace where there are certain consumers that would rather not spend that many dollars on their beef consumption."

Sustained, multiyear droughts are the primary reason for the rise in prices, Griffith said. As calves are weaned in the fall, ranchers must decide whether to retain their heifers to expand the herd or sell off the female calves. Drought conditions in multiple cattle-producing states have deteriorated pastures, and if ranchers don't have enough hay on hand to feed the herd they already have, they will opt to sell their heifers. This is largely why the national cattle herd is the smallest in 75 years .

At the same time, consumer demand for beef has grown 9 percent over the past decade, according to the Agriculture Department.

Domestic cattle shortages mean more beef is arriving from abroad — and it's more expensive, up from $4.96 per pound in June 2025 to $5.59 per pound in June 2026. The U.S. spent $26.3 billion on imported beef in 2025, 24 percent more than the previous year.

The Trump administration is trying to confront rising beef costs on at least two fronts. Earlier this year, the Justice Department's Antitrust Division sent letters to major retailers , looking into their beef prices and margins. In August, the president also issued a proclamation to allow more than 660 million pounds of lean beef trimmings to enter the country at a reduced tariff rate over the next three months. The meat is destined for the U.S. ground beef market, said Will Harris, owner of White Oak Pastures, a regenerative farm in Bluffton, Georgia, that has its own USDA-approved slaughterhouse.

The foreign beef is so lean it's "barely edible," Harris said. The meat will be combined with excess fat from U.S. slaughterhouses to create ground beef blends, with various fat-to-lean meat ratios.

"You take those two inedible products and you make ground beef out of it," Harris said.

The imports have been criticized by the National Cattlemen's Beef Association and politicians from cattle-producing states , saying they will hurt U.S. ranchers. Some have raised consumer safety issues about the meat and suggested it will only help the "big four" meatpackers that control about 85 percent of the beef market . But, mostly, critics say the foreign imports will do little to lower the price of ground beef.

Griffith, the University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture professor, said even if the U.S. brings in 660 million pounds of beef, that only represents about six weeks of added imports. "The needle's not going to move that much. " He said consumers might see ground beef prices drop by a "few cents" a pound.

On the restaurant level, operators are looking for ways to keep their burgers affordable, particularly at the kind of casual shops where diners expect a good, greasy and cheap meal. At Hamburger America in Manhattan, a double smash burger sells for $12.50, which is a dollar more than what the diner charged when it debuted nearly three years ago. The markup is less than a 10 percent increase, but Hamburger America pays 30 percent more for ground beef than when it opened, said Schnipper, the managing partner.

"Our view, generally, is we'd rather keep the prices a little bit tighter," Schnipper said. "We make a little less margin, but we're hoping to always make it up with volume."

At Shake Shack, the chain is walking a tightrope. It buys Angus beef from Pat LaFrieda Meat Purveyors, the reputable New Jersey company that sells only prime and upper levels of choice grade beef. Yet Shake Shack competes in a market in which consumers are looking for value as much as quality. As such, Meyer said, the chain can't afford to raise prices far above those at McDonald's or Burger King, even though the latter are not buying the same kind of beef. In Washington, a single-patty ShackBurger sells for about $8; a similar-sized Quarter Pounder from McDonald's goes for about $7.20.

Meyer wasn't certain but he thought Shake Shack had not raised prices on burgers so far this year, even as the price of beef has soared. (A spokesman for the chain declined to comment on prices.)

"Have beef prices gone up for Shake Shack? Absolutely," Meyer said. "But I can tell you that the team has done backflips trying to take cost out of everything else we do. "

In full-service restaurants, some owners are leaning into this new world of elevated burger prices by trading on expensive and custom ingredients. At Bar Angie in Washington's West End neighborhood, the native New Yorkers behind the bistro offer a triple-stack smash cheeseburger built with prime beef patties, which are tucked into a custom-made bun. The burger and hand-cut fries cost $35.

"We try really hard not to pass every increase along to our guests, but at some point we do have to adjust our pricing. And if we're going to charge $34 for a burger, we want to make sure we're giving our guests a burger that's actually worth it," co-owner Joe Ragonese said in an email, misquoting the price of his burger.

After learning about the burger inflation at Le Diplomate, Starr said he would look into changing the blend for his ground beef. He might switch from more expensive cuts, such as brisket and hanger, to ground chuck, a common ingredient in many grinds. If his team comes up with an acceptable — and cheaper — new blend, Starr said he would do something rarely seen at restaurants: He would lower the price of his burger.

articles.title: Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers say
articles.summary: Some 10 families had reportedly been living in the six-storey building in Gaza City that was hit by an Israeli strike last year.
articles.body:
Rescuers search for survivors with their bare hands

At least 21 people have been killed, including eight children, after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip overnight, rescuers and medics say.

Witnesses told the BBC that the six-storey building in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa area had been left tilting dangerously to one side after an Israeli strike more than a year ago. Displaced families had lived inside because they were desperate, they said.

UN and Egyptian teams joined the search for survivors, which was slow due to a lack of equipment. Initially, rescuers from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency had to use their bare hands.

On Wednesday afternoon, they said they had ended the operation after taking 45 injured people to hospitals.

Sherif, whose sister was killed, said: "They couldn't find a tent or somewhere to live.

"This was the last place they could turn to, despite the danger. They were aware that it would likely end in tragedy. A lack of resources drove them towards certain death."

A woman living in a tent nearby, Umm Mohammed Bakrun, said she had been talking to her son when the building collapsed suddenly in the early hours of Wednesday.

"It felt like an earthquake. There was a loud sound and I couldn't stand up. Stones rained down on us and when I looked outside I saw a lot of dust," she told the BBC. "Within minutes, there were screams everywhere."

Another witness, Mansour Abu Mohammed, said the building collapsed "in a few seconds".

"Every day, a stone or a few stones would fall from it, but the people inside couldn't find anywhere else to live. I used to live next door to it and you could see that it was tilting to one side."

Satellite imagery shows that the area around the building was targeted in the early weeks of the war, while damage to the building itself first became evident in 2024.

The head of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Gaza office, Alessandro Mrakic, told reporters at the scene on Wednesday morning that "the situation... is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed".

He also warned that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza were at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches.

"We need support, most importantly with machinery, equipment, among others. Our colleagues here don't have [engine] oil and spare parts to continue to work with all the equipment that is still in Gaza."

The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was "devastated" by the reports of the building collapse.

"No-one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he said.

He also urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries to Gaza of heavy machinery for rescue operations, as well as tents, tarpaulins and other non-food items for displaced people ahead of the winter rains.

Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups that could also have military uses.

An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.

More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.

The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed last October, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.

On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.

The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.

Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza. A spokesperson for the Israeli military told the BBC it was not aware of such an incident.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

articles.title: Germany to tackle welfare fraud through new 10-point plan
articles.summary: The German government has drawn up a 10-point plan of action to combat the abuse of social benefits to be implemented by the end of the year, dpa learned on...
articles.body:
The German government has drawn up a 10-point plan of action to combat the abuse of social benefits to be implemented by the end of the year, dpa learned on Wednesday.

The plan aims to reduce incentives for people to migrate to Germany in order to access its social welfare system, with the aim of ending large-scale abuse of the social benefit system.

The government also wants to make it easier to combat exploitative business models involving rundown or substandard properties used in schemes targeting vulnerable people.

The plan has been drawn up by the Labour and Social Affairs Ministry headed by Bärbel Bas, and the Interior Ministry under Alexander Dobrindt.

Bas said the aim was to give municipalities the power to take more effective action against substandard properties, with those behind organized exploitation held accountable.

articles.title: Fighting continues in Yemen's central Marib Province
articles.summary: Yemeni government forces bombarded Houthi targets in contested Marib Province, military sources reported on Wednesday. The internationally recognized governm...
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces bombarded Houthi targets in Marib Province in response to an attempted advance by the Iran-backed rebels.

Marib Province is strategically important due to its oil and gas reserves and its location connecting several provinces in central Yemen.

The recent offensive by the Houthis along the western coast has demonstrated the fragility of the alliance of pro-government forces in Yemen.

Yemeni government forces bombarded Houthi targets in contested Marib Province, military sources reported on Wednesday.

The internationally recognized government, which is supported by Saudi Arabia, used drones and artillery, in response to an attempted advance by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, according to the reports.

The Yemeni army released videos showing drone strikes on Houthi positions.

Marib has long been contested in Yemen's civil war and is a strategic target, partly because of its oil and gas reserves. Its location east of the Houthi-occupied capital of Sanaa makes Marib important as a hub connecting several provinces in the central part of the country.

As part of the recent offensive Houthi drive along the western coast, new fighting has also broken out on several fronts in Marib.

A government-allied militia in southern Yemen, known as the Giants Brigades, also reported fighting with the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Two Houthi vehicles were reportedly destroyed and their occupants killed.

The Houthis' rapid advance along the western coast has demonstrated the fragility of the alliance of pro-government forces in Yemen.

The so-called National Resistance Forces said the Houthis had prepared the operation for months and advanced with more than 70,000 fighters. They reportedly attacked with dozens of missiles, drones, and boats packed with explosives.

According to estimates from 2024, the Houthis have around 350,000 fighters.

articles.title: UK trade unions back motion to boycott and sanction Israel
articles.summary: Motion demands taking action to oppose the ‘catastrophic destruction of Gaza’ and Israeli settler violence.
articles.body:
The Trades Union Congress, representing over 5.3 million workers in the UK, has voted in favor of a motion supporting the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement against Israel.

The motion demands action to oppose the "catastrophic destruction of Gaza" and Israeli settler violence, including campaigning to end military cooperation and arms deals with Israel.

The vote puts additional pressure on the UK government to take a stronger stance against Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, despite Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's opposition to the BDS movement.

The umbrella organisation for trade unions in the United Kingdom has passed a motion calling for an end to complicity in Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and settler violence in the occupied West Bank.

The Trades Union Congress, representing more than 5.3 million workers, voted in favour of the motion on Wednesday during its annual conference in Brighton, southern England. The vote marks the first time the congress has backed the Palestinian-led movement Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions known as BDS .

"It's essential for the trade union movement to answer the call from the BDS movement, to challenge all complicity and to use our collective powers, to stand shoulder to shoulder with Palestinians to Free Palestine," said Zita Holborne from Artists' Union England, which put forward the motion.

The unanimous vote demands that the Trades Union Congress take action to oppose what the motion described as the "catastrophic destruction of Gaza" and Israeli settler violence "supported by the IDF [Israeli army]".

The steps include campaigning to end military cooperation and arms deals with Israel, calling on the government to impose wide-ranging sanctions on Israel and backing trade union-led campaigns in support of Palestine.

Co-founder of the BDS movement, Omar Barghouti, welcomed the development.

"This mass movement of solidarity with the people of Palestine, led by Palestine Solidarity Campaign with many trade unions affiliated to it, is the reason why your government was compelled to adopt minor measures in the right direction to end its complicity," Barghouti said.

"But it's way short of the UK's legal obligations to end complicity in genocide, in apartheid, in illegal occupation. So, we must work further to grow our BDS movement."

The motion puts additional pressure on the government to take a stronger stance against Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Last week, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a ban on importing goods from Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law. Addressing Parliament, Miliband denounced "settler terrorists" for carrying out what he described as "ethnic cleansing" in parts of the West Bank.

However, the foreign secretary said he "wholeheartedly" opposes BDS, stressing that the UK would continue to "support important and valued trade" with Israel that adheres to international law.

Peter Leary, deputy director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, told Al Jazeera that Wednesday's vote marked a "tipping point".

"In marked contrast to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's attempt to dismiss the Palestinian BDS movement, trade unions are paving the way to secure real change, and we must keep up the pressure to force the government to take meaningful action and end all military, diplomatic and economic support for Israel," he said.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the Trades Union Congress and the UK government but did not receive a response at the time of publication.

articles.title: Ex-BBC presenter John Humphrys questions role of Royal Family in new documentary
articles.summary: John Humphrys, who presented Today and the Nine O'Clock News, heads a new Channel 4 documentary on the topic.
articles.body:
Veteran broadcaster John Humphrys has said the people of the United Kingdom should "be able to choose our leaders" as he releases a documentary exploring the role of the Royal Family.

Humphrys, who for decades was one of the most prominent faces on the BBC, is presenting a new Channel 4 documentary called The Royals: Time to Go?

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast , the Cardiff-born presenter said he "admires" King Charles III in many ways, but said it was a "matter of choice".

Buckingham Palace has been approached for comment.

In the documentary, Humphrys speaks to both critics and supporters of the monarchy, and makes the case for electing a president as the head of state.

He recalled seeing the late Queen Elizabeth II visiting Cardiff when he was growing up, watching her being driven down Newport Road.

"My father didn't attend and said he would never bend the knee to anyone. I guess that rubbed off on me," he said.

Humphrys asked why it was seen as such a taboo to call for an alternative to the Royal Family, saying that "we can because it's a democracy".

"I know the monarch is not a political leader, but he is our leader, and we need to bow our knee to him.

"That's what I object to. Shouldn't we get a choice?"

He met the Queen throughout his career, including at Buckingham Palace where he said he spoke to her "and the corgis of course".

Humphrys, who presented the Nine O'Clock News, the Today programme and Mastermind throughout a decades-long career with the corporation, said he took the opportunity to ask her for an interview.

"When I'd finished, she looked up at me and said just one word 'no' and I thought I could build on that," he said.

articles.title: Nobel laureate Narges Mohammadi’s memoir details abuse in Iranian prison. She says she’s prepared for the consequences
articles.summary: During her incarceration at Tehran’s notorious Evin prison, Nobel peace laureate Narges Mohammadi would smuggle out fragments of writing with the help of her friends and fellow inmates.
articles.body: During her incarceration at Tehran’s notorious Evin prison, Nobel peace laureate Narges Mohammadi would smuggle out fragments of writing with the help of her friends and fellow inmates. The risks were enormous; Mohammadi, 54, has suffered violent beatings, fallen gravely ill and spent much of the last two decades in prison, away from her children, for her activism against the Iranian regime. “One of my friends was trying to take out just three sheets of paper on a visiting day, but the prison security forces confiscated them from her,” Mohammadi told CNN’s Jomana Karadsheh Wednesday in one of her first interviews since being released from prison in May on temporary medical leave. Another time, more than 20 of her notebooks were lost after she says she was badly beaten and exiled to another prison. But she kept writing, unafraid of the costs of speaking out, and has turned those fragments into a memoir “A Woman Never Stops Fighting,” which is being released this month in some European countries. In the book, Mohammadi shares new details about the people responsible for her mistreatment in prison. “In order to document these things, it is better to speak openly about their methods, to expose and reveal their torture,” she said, wearing a multi-colored dress with the word “peace” printed in different languages and sitting in front of a portrait of Mahsa Jhina Amini, who was killed after being held in custody by Iran’s morality police, sparking nationwide protests in the autumn of 2022. Publishing a book like this is dangerous. “There may be consequences, but this is what life is like for us in this region and in this country,” she said. She also acknowledged the risk of retribution for talking to CNN, but said she wasn’t worried and that it was her “duty” to speak out. To avoid putting her at further risk, CNN agreed to focus the interview on her new memoir and personal experiences rather than recent events in Iran. “If I could go back to the moment when I began my struggle, to each and every moment when I was arrested, even knowing what would happen to me, I would certainly make the same choice to begin the struggle,” she said. “But when I look at Ali and Kiana,” she added, referencing her now 19-year-old twins, “I find myself filled with doubt. Did I really have the right to deprive them of a very ordinary life, of having their mother with them? That is the difficult part of the question, and I cannot answer it with certainty.” In total, Mohammadi, one of Iran’s most prominent human rights activists, has been sentenced to more than 44 years in prison as well as 154 lashes, according to her foundation. During her most recent stint behind bars between December and May, she endured beatings and “life-threatening mistreatment,” the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in February, citing “credible reports.” Those reports said she was beaten repeatedly with wooden sticks and batons during her arrest in December and dragged across the ground by her hair, sustaining injuries that left open wounds on her head. She was also kicked repeatedly in the pelvis and genital area, leaving her in severe pain and unable to sit or function normally, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, told CNN in February. “I was held in solitary confinement for two months in that same condition, without being allowed to make phone calls or see my family or even my lawyers,” Mohammadi recalled. She suffered a suspected heart attack in March, lost 20 kilograms (44 pounds) of weight and her condition deteriorated so much that her life was “in imminent danger,” her foundation warned in April. After months of neglect by authorities, she was hospitalized for 18 days, suffering from heart disease caused by chronic anxiety and stress, her foundation said. At the time, Tasnim, one of Iran’s semi-official state news agencies, rejected reports her condition had deteriorated. Eventually, Mohammadi was discharged and temporarily allowed to return home. She says she is still receiving medical treatment. Keeping prisoners in solitary confinement is “one of the government’s tools,” to “destroy a person” rather than simply executing them, Mohammadi said. The aim is to “break them down psychologically, emotionally and physically; to strip them of their identity, to strip them of their humanity, and to distort and undermine their perceptions,” she said. Denying prisoners timely access to medical treatment is “another method that seriously endangers their health and, in some cases, leads to their death,” she said. “These deaths are a form of silent execution.” The Iranian government and official media have downplayed Mohammadi’s allegations of mistreatment, despite eyewitness accounts and international public outcry. Despite the risks that come with opposing the regime, two large-scale protest movements have convulsed Iran in recent years – one in January and one in the autumn of 2022 that was prompted by the death of 22-year-old Amini. Both were met with violent crackdowns from authorities. “If you look at the streets of Tehran, and even at cities across the country, you can see how courageously women are standing tall in the streets,” Mohammadi said. “Through the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, we were able to create the power of the protestor and present it to the world; that is, someone who had come out into the streets would be beaten, killed, imprisoned and executed, but they had a sense of power, a sense of legitimacy which forced the government to retreat.” For Mohammadi, constantly straddling the dual identities of a mother and an activist, her book represents both a paean to those fighting for democracy as well as the “words of a mother who wrote this book in prison,” with her children living far way in exile in France. “Ali and Kiana have always been the force that brought me back to life and kept me hopeful,” she said. “I hope to see them, embrace them, and see how much they have grown – to see whether I come up to their shoulders now, or they come up to mine – and to stand beside them again.”

articles.title: Ozzy Osbourne's final Black Sabbath performance set for cinemas
articles.summary: Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back To The Beginning is released on 28 October in cinemas worldwide.
articles.body:
Ozzy Osbourne's final ever performance with Black Sabbath, filmed just 17 days before his death, is set to be shown in cinemas.

The Birmingham-born star, known as the Prince of Darkness, died aged 76 in July 2025, after Sabbath's Back To The Beginning farewell concert , where he was reunited in the city with his bandmates for the first time in 20 years.

The show, which saw them joined by an array of metal artists who regard them as heroes including Metallica, Guns 'n' Roses and Anthrax, gets a worldwide cinema release on 28 October.

Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back To The Beginning captures Osbourne with the band's original line-up, guitarist Tony Iommi, bassist Geezer Butler and drummer Bill Ward.

It has been produced by Mercury Studios, whose co-leads Ken Danquah and Andrea Dunn said: "Ozzy Osbourne is one of the most influential figures in music history, and his final performance with Black Sabbath deserves to be seen on the biggest possible stage.

"Last year, we brought this legendary concert to fans across the globe, offering millions the chance to be there through an unprecedented livestream.

"This film is the next chapter, giving fans a new way to experience that night on the big screen.

"Back To The Beginning captures the scale of a stadium performance and the intimacy of a farewell, crafted specifically for the cinema screen."

The sold out show at Villa Park stadium also saw Osborne perform a solo set with material from his career that saw him sell more than 55 million albums, after he was sacked from Sabbath in 1979.

Hosted by Jason Momoa with Rage Against The Machine guitarist Tom Morello serving as musical director, the show also included sets from bands including Guns N Roses and Metallica.

During the concert Osbourne – who was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2019 – told the crowd: "I don't know what to say, man, I've been laid up for like six years. You have no idea how I feel – thank-you from the bottom of my heart."

His wife Sharon said the concert came about after she asked her husband "what would really make him happy".

"He said the only thing that would make him happy was if he could perform again and say goodbye to his fans," she said.

"That's all he wanted to do. He wanted to say goodbye and thank-you."

Iommi called the event "closure for the band", while Ward said he felt "completely at home" on stage again with his bandmates.

"To me it was like pure love," Butler said.

"It was just a wave of love. It's the only way I can describe it really. I mean I could feel it as if it is like tangible."

The band has been widely credited with defining and popularising the sound of heavy metal.

Osbourne also appeared in 2000s reality TV series The Osbournes, alongside wife Sharon and their two youngest children.

articles.title: At 23, Ben Bell became New Zealand's youngest mayor by just 8 votes; after a no-confidence fight, he won re-election in 2025
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At 23, Ben Bell entered New Zealand local government with one of the narrowest mayoral victories in recent Gore history. He had defeated six-term incu.
articles.body: At 23, Ben Bell entered New Zealand local government with one of the narrowest mayoral victories in recent Gore history. He had defeated six-term incumbent Tracy Hicks by eight votes, a margin so small that the result was challenged in court. A judge later declined Hicks’ request for a recount, confirming Bell as the country’s youngest local body mayor.That first victory was only the beginning of a difficult term. Bell’s relationship with members of the Gore District Council deteriorated, while his working relationship with chief executive Stephen Parry also became strained. Councillors eventually sought his resignation and a no-confidence motion was prepared, although it was not put to a vote.Three years later, Bell returned to the ballot. This time, the result was considerably clearer.An eight-vote margin made Bell mayor at 23The 2022 Gore mayoral contest was unusually close. Bell, standing as the Team Hokonui candidate, received 2,371 votes, while Hicks received 2,363. The eight-vote difference represented only a fraction of the votes cast, as reported by Radio News Zealand (RNZ).Hicks sought a judicial recount, pointing to the number of informal and blank voting papers. The application was considered by District Court Judge J D Kelly, who rejected the request. In his findings, Kelly said the evidence presented did not establish a sufficient basis for ordering a recount.The judge also considered the possible effect of disputed voting papers. Even if certain votes had gone to Hicks, the evidence did not account for the additional votes he would have needed to overturn Bell’s majority. The recount application therefore did not alter the result. Bell could then take up the office formally. At 23, he became New Zealand’s youngest local body mayor.The new mayor arrived with a ‘back to basics’ agendaBell entered the role talking about practical local issues rather than a sweeping programme. His campaign had focused on matters including rural roads, water infrastructure and recycling, alongside his wider call for a return to what he described as the basics of local government.The transition into office was immediate. Before even being sworn in, Bell had official engagements connected with the district, including the first sod-turning for Mercury’s Kaiwera Downs wind farm and the Gore District Community Awards. He also planned to meet council staff and begin briefings with councillors.At the time, Bell spoke about working with the new council as a united group and keeping communication with residents open. The narrow election result had produced a mayor, but it also left him facing the practical task of governing alongside councillors who had not all supported his campaign.Relations inside the council soon became difficultThe problems that followed were not simply about Bell's age or the closeness of his election. His relationship with other elected members became increasingly strained during the first months of his term.By 2023, the dispute had become public. Seven of Gore's 10 councillors asked Bell to resign, saying they had lost confidence in his leadership. The conflict was also intertwined with the deteriorating relationship between Bell and council chief executive Stephen Parry.A proposed vote of no confidence in Bell was ultimately not taken. Instead, councillors agreed to work with Local Government New Zealand on an independent process aimed at rebuilding confidence in the council. Bell supported the amended motion. There were disagreements over governance, communication and the relationship between the mayor and chief executive. At one stage, the mayor and Parry were communicating through an intermediary, while external mediation was used to try to repair the working relationship.The conflict became a defining part of his first termThe turbulence continued to follow Bell into the later part of his first three years in office. In 2024, he acknowledged that he had considered resigning during the period of intense pressure, although he ultimately remained mayor. He said at the time that he did not believe stepping aside was fair to the community.The dispute also led to wider changes within the council. Parry eventually left the chief executive position, and a new chief executive was appointed. Mediation and an independent review were among the measures used as the council attempted to move beyond the breakdown in relationships.By the time the 2025 local elections approached, Bell was seeking another term with a record that was considerably more complicated than the eight-vote victory that had first brought him into office.Bell returned to the ballot in 2025The 2025 mayoral contest gave Gore voters a choice between Bell and former district councillor and businesswoman Nicky Davis. The Gore District Council confirmed the two candidates when nominations closed in August.Bell's first term was a central part of the campaign backdrop. His disagreements with councillors and the former chief executive had received national attention, while Bell himself rejected some of the characterisation of his time in office and defended his record. RNZ reported in July 2025 that he described coverage of his first term as bullying.The election therefore offered a very different measure of support from his first contest. In 2022, Bell had won by eight votes. In 2025, there was no need for a recount application or a legal dispute over a handful of ballots.Bell’s 2025 victory was far wider than his eight-vote win in 2022According to Gore District Council, the final 2025 result showed Bell with 3,392 votes, compared with 1,508 for Davis. One informal voting paper and 90 blank papers were also recorded. Gore District Council declared Bell elected for another three-year term.The result was significant in numerical terms because it bore little resemblance to the razor-thin margin of 2022. Bell secured more than twice as many votes as his opponent in the final count.The council's official figures also recorded voter turnout at 54.82% after special votes were included, the highest turnout recorded for the Gore District's local elections. Bell was 26 by the time of his second election. He remained the youngest mayor in the country, but his position was no longer based on an eight-vote contest.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump praises PM Modi for curbing ‘illicit opium cultivation’ as India stays on US ‘drug transit’ list
articles.summary: India News: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday welcomed Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to curb illicit opium poppy cultivation in India, even as Washi.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday welcomed Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to curb illicit opium poppy cultivation in India, even as Washington included India among 23 countries designated as major drug transit or illicit drug-producing countries.In a Presidential Determination submitted to the US Congress, Trump said he looked forward to continued cooperation with India under the United States-India Drug Policy Framework. “I welcome Prime Minister Modi and the Government of India’s efforts to address illicit opium poppy cultivation and bolster supply chain integrity,” Trump said in the directive made public on Wednesday.India’s inclusion on the list does not, however, amount to a US finding that its government is failing to tackle the drug trade. The determination said countries are designated because of a combination of geographic, commercial and economic factors that allow illicit drugs or precursor chemicals to be produced or moved through their territory.The US document specifically noted that being placed on the list does not necessarily reflect a country’s current counterdrug efforts or the extent of its cooperation with Washington.Along with India, the countries identified by the US include Afghanistan, The Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Burma, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Jamaica, Laos, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Pakistan, Peru, Venezuela and China.The designation comes as Washington continues to focus on disrupting international drug supply chains, including the movement of precursor chemicals used to manufacture synthetic drugs. The White House’s 2026 National Drug Control Strategy has also called for stronger bilateral counterdrug cooperation with countries including India.Trump highlights US-India cooperationTrump said the US and India would continue working together on counter-narcotics efforts. The two countries established a Drug Policy Executive Working Group earlier this year, with discussions focused on illicit narcotics trafficking, precursor chemicals and the security of pharmaceutical supply chains.The US president also pointed to what he described as “historic progress” by his administration in tackling drug trafficking and narcoterrorist organisations.He cited tighter border security, lower drug seizures and a decline in overdose deaths as evidence of progress, saying seizures of fentanyl and other drugs along the US southern border had fallen by more than half after what he called four years of “open border chaos”.“After four years of open border chaos, seizures of fentanyl and other drugs being smuggled into the United States have been reduced by more than half, and drug overdose deaths have plunged,” Trump said.Trump presses China over drug precursorsTrump separately called on China to take stronger action against the flow of precursor chemicals used to manufacture fentanyl, methamphetamine and other synthetic drugs.“The PRC continues to be the world’s largest producer of many of the precursor chemicals used to illicitly produce fentanyl, methamphetamine, and other deadly synthetic drugs,” Trump said.He said he had raised the issue directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping and noted that Beijing had introduced licensing requirements last year for companies exporting designated precursor chemicals to North America.The US has made disruption of precursor-chemical supply chains a central part of its broader counter-drug strategy, which calls for international cooperation to prevent legitimate trade channels from being exploited for illicit drug production.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Utah couple spent 14 years trying to stop their 25.5-acre farm from becoming another subdivision; the land is now permanently protected from development even as homes spread around it
articles.summary: US News: A stretch of green farmland surrounded by growing communities can look increasingly out of place, but one Utah couple spent years ensuring their prope.
articles.body: A stretch of green farmland surrounded by growing communities can look increasingly out of place, but one Utah couple spent years ensuring their property would remain that way. Sheri Schiess and her late husband, Boyd, worked for 14 years to preserve their 25.5-acre farm in Nibley, Utah, as development expanded around it. According to a report by Utah Public Radio (UPR), their effort ultimately resulted in a conservation easement with the Bear River Land Conservancy, permanently removing most development rights from the property. The agreement means the farm can continue to be used for agriculture, but it cannot be turned into a subdivision by Schiess, her children or future generations.A farm surrounded by developmentThe Schiess property sits at the corner of 4000 South and 640 West in Nibley, an area where development has been advancing. Yet the farm itself remains an open expanse of agricultural land, with hay grown on the property and sheep being fed from it. For Schiess, preserving that landscape is about more than simply keeping an undeveloped patch of land. She lives only a few blocks away and continues to use the farm as working agricultural ground. She also uses wool from her sheep in educational activities, including teaching schoolchildren how to dye it.The effort to protect the property began years before the final conservation agreement was reached. Schiess told Utah Public Radio that the process took 14 years and involved a lengthy bureaucratic process. Her husband, Boyd, died not long after the couple entered the agreement in 2022. The conservation easement now ensures that the land will remain protected regardless of who owns it in the future. Under the agreement, the development rights were largely donated, meaning the property remains privately owned while its potential for future development is permanently restricted.How a conservation easement worksA conservation easement does not necessarily mean that land becomes a public park. Instead, it places permanent restrictions on how the property can be developed while allowing the owner to retain ownership and continue approved uses.In the Schiess case, the land remains a working farm. There is also no guarantee that the public will be allowed onto the property. That distinction is important because conservation does not always mean creating publicly accessible open space. According to Utah Public Radio, Gabriel Murray, executive director of the Bear River Land Conservancy, said that some properties are better suited to remaining private agricultural land while still providing conservation benefits. Wildlife habitat and waterways can also be protected through easements even when the public does not have access.The Bear River Land Conservancy, founded in 2011, uses government and donor funding to acquire development rights from properties in the region. In cases such as Schiess' farm, the approach allows land to remain privately owned while preventing future conversion to development.Why Utah is using the approachConservation easements are becoming more common in Cache Valley as communities face the challenge of preserving open land while development continues. One reason is cost. Buying an entire property can be considerably different from purchasing only its development rights. Christopher Sands, a member of the Cache Open Space Advisory Committee, told the Salt Lake Tribune that purchasing an easement essentially means buying the development rights off the property. That can allow public money and private conservation funding to protect more land without governments taking ownership of every acre.There are examples elsewhere in Utah as well. Cache County purchased nearly 800 acres in the Sherwood Hills area in Wellsville in 2025. That $7.5 million transaction included 471 acres that were made available to the public, while another 300 privately owned acres were placed under a conservation easement. Park City has also combined outright ownership with conservation easements as part of its open-space preservation efforts. City officials have said Park City owns thousands of acres of open space, while additional land is protected through easements.A piece of farmland that will stay greenFor Schiess, the result is particularly personal. The farm is part of her late husband's family's agricultural legacy, and the agreement means the open landscape will remain visible even as the surrounding area changes. The arrangement also illustrates a broader question facing growing communities: whether preserving open land necessarily requires turning it into publicly owned space. In this case, the answer was to leave the farm in private hands while permanently removing its development potential.Schiess can continue growing hay and caring for her sheep, while the property remains protected for future generations. The agreement does not stop development elsewhere in Nibley, but it ensures that these 25.5 acres will not become another residential subdivision. After 14 years of trying to secure that outcome, the farm has a future that looks very different from the development spreading around it: it will remain agricultural land, protected by a conservation easement that runs with the property rather than ending with its current owner.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Norfolk police commissioner cancels 'ridiculous' theatre tour
articles.summary: Colin Sutton tells a meeting that he has pulled out of a 127-date tour due to residents' reaction.
articles.body:
An under-fire £79,000-a-year police commissioner said he had cancelled heavily criticised plans to take part in a 127-date national theatre tour.

Opposition parties had questioned how Reform UK's Colin Sutton would be able to oversee Norfolk Police while also presenting a live true crime stage show across the UK.

Sutton told a council meeting that the number of dates was "ridiculous" and that he had pulled out of the "Makings of a Murderer" tour after being contacted by residents.

Conservative Matthew Taylor, who stood against Sutton in the police and crime commissioner election in July, said it had been "a sorry saga".

A high profile former detective who led the investigation to catch Levi Bellfield, the murderer of Milly Dowler, Marsha McDonnell and Amelie Delagrange, Sutton comfortably won the election to become Norfolk's commissioner two months ago.

A regular on TV documentaries, he has previously carried out a long national theatre tour talking about his career.

Last week, promoters announced his follow-up series of shows would take place next year and Sutton initially said it "wouldn't impinge" on his day job.

But on Tuesday, he admitted to the BBC that he was considering cancelling the tour and on Wednesday he told councillors he had now scrapped it.

"What surprised me and what made me reflect and think again was the reaction that I got personally from a number of residents," he told North Norfolk District Council's scrutiny committee.

"I'm not sure I could do 127 dates because it was ridiculous, but I could have done some. What I don't want to do is to give the impression to anybody that I don't take this role seriously and I'm not going to do a good job on this.

"So that's why my decision has been: OK, I'm not legally obliged to do this, I'm not going to do it."

Taylor, a county councillor who came second to Sutton in the commissioner election, said it had "been a sorry saga, one that erodes public confidence in those who are supposed to represent them".

"I know many people across Norfolk have been deeply disappointed by this episode," he added.

South Norfolk Labour MP Ben Goldsborough also said it was "good" that Sutton had pulled out.

"But the fact it took a huge public backlash to make him realise that being Norfolk's police and crime commissioner should come before his career as a touring personality tells its own story," he said.

The promoters of the show, Entertainers, have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Oregon settles with Christian mother denied foster care adoption over gender identity beliefs
articles.summary: Jessica Bates said Oregon denied her foster care adoption application after she refused to use preferred pronouns or take a child to hormone therapy.
articles.body: A widowed Oregon mother of five who hoped to give a home to a child in foster care and says she was shut out of the process after telling state officials her Christian beliefs prevented her from affirming a child’s gender transition has reached a settlement with the state allowing her to continue pursuing adoption. Jessica Bates told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that she completed Oregon’s foster care training after deciding to pursue adoption but raised what she described as conflicts of conscience with requirements concerning gender identity and the care of children who identify as LGBTQ+. "In the training, the state wanted me to be willing to put pride flags around the house or if a child should come into my care that didn't identify as binary or whatnot, then I would need to affirm their identity, use their preferred pronouns, support this behavior even if it conflicted with my faith and what I hold to be true," Bates said. CHRISTIAN LIFEGUARD WHO REFUSED PRIDE FLAG DUTIES AND WAS SUSPENDED IS NOW HEADED TOWARD TRIAL "When I was on the phone call with them a few months later, they basically kind of set up the litmus test that, ‘OK, well, what if we place a child in your care who wants to transition from one sex to the other, and we want — we need you to take this child to hormone injection appointments. Would you be willing to do that?’" Bates said they asked. "And that was kind of the straw that broke the camel's back, because I absolutely would not be willing to do that." Bates began the process to become certified to adopt in March 2022 from Oregon’s foster care system, but in September 2022 she was denied her application by Oregon due to her religious beliefs, according to Alliance Defending Freedom, which has represented Bates. ONE OF NATION'S LARGEST CHRISTIAN FOSTER AGENCIES WILL NOT ALLOW LGBTQ COUPLES TO ADOPT CHILDREN Bates said she told officials that gender affirmation for a child who believes he or she is a different gender than what they were born with is "child abuse," and society has yet to learn the full effects of gender transition hormones. "It was hard being told you can't adopt or help at all when you know that there were literally like a few thousand kids out there in the foster care system," Bates said. "And just knowing, nope, you can't help, and you're excluded was really hard. "And, you've probably heard, I am a widow," she added. "My husband was killed in 2017 in a head-on collision. That's kind of a long story in itself, but my five kids and I know what it is to have grief and to lose someone that you love. "And just the idea that there's these kids out here, at the same time, while I'm seeing my kids kind of go through life without their dad. And to know there's kids out there that don't have a parent, either want mom or dad that's able to invest in them and love them." EXCLUSIVE: INDIANA SCHOOL COUNSELOR FIRED FOR SPEAKING OUT ON GENDER IDENTITY POLICY SETTLES LAWSUIT FOR $200K In March 2023, ADF filed a federal complaint on her behalf, and in December 2023, following a federal district court ruling against Bates, ADF appealed her case to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, asking the court to allow her to access Oregon’s adoption system without discrimination while her lawsuit continues. In July 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled that Bates can start the process of adopting siblings from foster care without violating her religious beliefs about human sexuality while her lawsuit against state officials progresses. "This settlement will allow me to continue in the process of looking to foster, to adopt," Bates said. "I plan to do that even though my family life has changed a lot in the last four years. I became a grandmother. My oldest son's married, and he's actually — they're living with me, just because cost of living and everything is so high right now, but I would like to continue the process and this case allows me to do that." articles.title: Lebanon returns 37 artefacts smuggled out of Egypt six years ago
articles.summary: The artefacts date back to the pharaonic civilisation, more commonly referred to as ancient Egypt.
articles.body:
Lebanon has returned 37 artefacts to Egypt that were smuggled out of the country six years ago.

A ceremony was held at the National Museum of Beirut in the Lebanese capital on Wednesday to celebrate the handover of the artefacts, which date back to the pharaonic civilisation, more commonly referred to as ancient Egypt.

“After investigating the identity and ownership of these items, it was determined that they belonged to Egypt,” said Lebanon’s Culture Minister Ghassan Salame as he gave the items to Egyptian Ambassador to Lebanon Alaa Moussa.

“We are setting an example in the strict implementation of the 1970 international convention concerning the prevention of the illicit trafficking of cultural property,” he was quoted as saying by Lebanon’s National News Agency.

The artefacts were seized from the Port of Beirut in 2020. Lebanon spent years working with INTERPOL, Egypt and the country’s top public prosecutor to verify the ownership and authenticity of the items.

The collection consists of masks, wooden dolls, pieces of Coptic textiles, amulets made from glass paste, medium-sized statues and two wooden coffins decorated with colourful designs.

Laura Salloum, an official with Lebanon’s Directorate General of Antiquities, said the artefacts had been purchased by a Lebanese national without official documentation confirming their source.

Such items are regularly stolen from Egypt. Last month, 48 artefacts were returned to Cairo by the FBI Art Crime Team in the United States.

Egypt’s official press office announced on Wednesday that its embassy in the Swiss capital, Bern, had recovered an ancient golden mummy mask with the help of local authorities.

articles.title: Meet Ollie Brunskill, the 10-year-old Launceston boy who spotted a kitchen fire, carried his baby sister outside and later received a Tasmanian government bravery award
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A 10-year-old boy in Tasmania became a real-life hero just a day after dressing up as his favourite video game character for Book Week. Ollie Brunskil.
articles.body: A 10-year-old boy in Tasmania became a real-life hero just a day after dressing up as his favourite video game character for Book Week. Ollie Brunskill was dressed as Link from The Legend of Zelda when he alerted his family to a fire in their home in Prospect Vale, northern Tasmania, and helped get his baby sister to safety.According to ABC News, the fire broke out in the family’s kitchen after a mandoline slicer was accidentally left on a hot plate. The flames quickly spread, but Ollie noticed the fire through the reflection of a kitchen window.Rather than panic, Ollie immediately alerted his mother, Stacey Brunskill, and then rushed to get his baby sister, Nora, out of the house.“My son came over and alerted me that there was a fire,” Stacey said.“I came out to see what was going on and there was probably about a half-metre-high flame on the stove at that point.”She said Ollie quickly got Nora out of her therapy chair, carried her outside and took her to a neighbour’s house.Fire blanket helps contain growing flamesStacey managed to smother the growing fire using a fire blanket, which she said she was “so grateful” to have at home.“The fire brigade said that's what stopped it from expanding further ... if I didn't have that, chances are that my house would have been completely demolished,” she said.By then, the house had filled with black smoke. After calling Triple Zero (000), Stacey retrieved a fire extinguisher from her car and used it through the kitchen window.“I managed to blast it through my kitchen window and get the fire out enough for my neighbour to run over and put the hose through the window,” she said.Although the fire was contained to the kitchen, smoke and soot damaged or ruined many belongings throughout the house.“Every door in the house was open ... my son's new bedding through to my daughter's new playpen and car seat, all of that was in the lounge room,” Stacey said.‘If Oliver hadn’t been here, we might not even be here’Despite the damage, Stacey believes the outcome could have been far worse without her son’s quick thinking.“If Oliver hadn't been here ... we might not even be here,” she said.Ollie’s actions were later recognised when he received a certificate of bravery from Education Minister Jo Palmer in front of his primary school on Wednesday.For the 10-year-old, the recognition had special meaning because of the character he had dressed up as just a day earlier.Ollie says Link inspired himOllie said he admires Link because he is “someone who saves people and species”.“Since Link's a hero, that next day I became a hero,” he said.“And I have long hair so I can dress up like him.”Ollie recalled seeing the kitchen engulfed in flames but said he was able to remain calm because he felt prepared.“Instead of grabbing everything which I really wanted to, I grabbed my baby sister,” he said.“I stayed calm so my mum would stay calm.”“Saving my baby sister wasn't on my bucket list,” he added.The 10-year-old also had a message for other children, urging them never to play with fire.“And make sure nothing is on your stove unless you're cooking, but have an adult help you,” he said.School praises Ollie’s braverySummerdale Primary School acting principal Toby O’Connor praised Ollie, describing him as a child with a “heart of gold”.He said staff and students were filled with “amazement and immense pride” following the incident.“We're very lucky, as most government schools are, to have fire education in school,” O’Connor said.“We've had that in the last couple of months ... I know after listening to Ollie and what he was able to do, that's a result of his bravery but also the education he's been able to gain from those valuable sessions.”Mother urges families to keep fire-safety equipment at homeStacey encouraged parents with young children to invest in basic fire-safety equipment, including fire blankets and extinguishers.She said she was “exceptionally proud” of her son.“More than I can ever put into words,” she said.Stacey also shared that Ollie has level two autism and ADHD and said she was especially proud that he was able to remain focused during the emergency.“He's pretty awesome because he also has level two autism and ADHD and is usually very full on and getting criticised for not paying enough attention to things,” she said.“He's the one that has saved us from potentially not being here.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Efforts underway for Zelenskyy-Trump meeting at UN next week
articles.summary: Trump pushes for a solution to end Moscow’s war against Kyiv as civilian deaths in Ukraine rise.
articles.body:
Efforts are underway to organise a “meaningful” meeting between United States President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during the United Nations General Assembly next week.

Ukrainian and US diplomatic teams are “actively” working to set up a meeting between Zelenskyy and Trump at the 81st UN General Assembly session in New York, according to press briefing by Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi.

Tykhyi said Zelenskyy’s visit will include dozens of bilateral negotiations and engagements with US legislators, business leaders and the Ukrainian community in the US.

Zelenskyy and Trump last met at the White House in July in a much-anticipated encounter after a heated 2025 televised meeting at the Oval Office ended abruptly, with US Vice President JD Vance calling Zelenskyy “disrespectful” for not thanking the US for its support for Ukraine.

As Ukrainian officials were preparing for the UN visit, a Russian drone strike on a bus killed at least five people and injured seven others on Wednesday in the city of Nikopol near the southern Ukraine front line.

The number of civilians killed in Ukraine has increased sharply this year , according to the UN, amid an escalation in Russian strikes. At least 1,396 civilians were killed and 7,978 wounded in Ukraine during the first six months of 2026, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, a 37 percent increase from the same period in the previous year.

Along with the Iran conflict, the war in Ukraine is also having an impact on diesel prices, according to the International Energy Agency.

Last week, Trump urged Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks were to blame for a global fuel shortage that was driving up prices, not the war with Iran.

And on Sunday, Trump said the increase in the price of diesel “isn’t done by the Middle East, this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine”.

Zelenskyy says Ukraine is ready to halt its attacks on Russian territory if the US can secure a commitment from Moscow to not hit Ukrainian infrastructure.

articles.title: Syria abolishes al-Assad-era ‘terrorism’ court as Kurdish tensions flare
articles.summary: Discontent is testing President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s ability to unify a country emerging from 14 years of conflict.
articles.body:
Syria’s parliament ‌has voted to abolish an al-Assad-era “terrorism” court and nullify the ⁠legal effects of ⁠its rulings, in one of the first significant legislative moves by the country’s new assembly .

The vote on Wednesday formalised the abolition of the court, which Syria’s new authorities had already treated as defunct, state-run Al-Ekhbariya TV reported.

The Counter-Terrorism Court, ⁠established in 2012, was used to prosecute thousands of Syrians for offences deemed “terrorism-related” ⁠under ousted former President Bashar al-Assad.

Wednesday’s vote came during the opening ⁠weeks of the first parliament formed since al-Assad was toppled. The chamber convened for the first time in July .

In June 2025, President Ahmed al-Sharaa issued a decree dismissing 67 judges who had served in what he described at the time as the “abolished ‌Counter-Terrorism Court”.

Syria’s March 2025 constitutional declaration had also called for abolishing the effects of what it described as unjust rulings issued by the court, including returning confiscated property.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee said in 2024 that the 2012 law establishing the court failed to adequately provide key judicial guarantees and raised concerns over arbitrary detention, torture or ill-treatment, and the court’s independence.

The vote is among the assembly’s first major legislative decisions after it ‌spent its initial sessions establishing its internal rules and committees.

The 53-year-long rule of the al-Assad family ended on December 8, 2024, after a lightning 11-day offensive that took Syria and the world by surprise. With it ended a brutal police state, notorious for its use of torture and disappearances .

Kurdish discontent amid government integration deal

Hundreds of oil tanker trucks were stranded in northeastern Syria’s Kurdish region on Wednesday after demonstrators blocked a major highway near the town of Tal Tamr in protest over rising fuel prices.

Discontent has been building in the Kurdish region amid a push to integrate a once-powerful Kurd-led armed force – the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) – into Syria’s army and bring them under the control of the central government.

The integration agreement with the SDF, minted in August, has been widely regarded as a victory for al-Sharaa’s government, but discontent is testing the president’s ability to unify a country emerging from 14 years of conflict.

Kurds, who made up about 10 percent of Syria’s population of 23 million before the civil war began in 2011, were long marginalised under the country’s al-Assad dynasty. During the war, they carved out a de facto autonomous zone in the northeast.

When northeast Syria – including its oilfields – was under the SDF’s control, fuel was heavily subsidised. After the central government took control, it removed those subsidies, leading to a price hike.

Syrian Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir is scheduled to be questioned in parliament on Thursday over the increase in fuel prices.

On Sunday, the government further hiked petrol prices by about 30 percent and diesel by 40 percent, citing rising global fuel prices due to the US-Israel war on Iran as well as repair work at the Baniyas refinery on the country’s coast.

Demonstrators shut down the M4 highway near the town of Tal Tamr, blocking trucks bringing oil from the Qamishli and Rmeilan oilfields, and announced that they would only reopen the route if the price increases were reversed.

Additionally, students in the cities of Qamishli and Hasakah staged mass protests in recent weeks over a government decree that makes Kurdish an official language of instruction for the first time in Syrian history but only provides for three classes a week in the language. By contrast, Kurds had set up a school system teaching mostly in Kurdish.

With the new post-war government reasserting control over the northeast, Kurdish communities have been anxious about losing the rights they had under self-rule. Al-Sharaa has promised constitutional protection for Kurdish language and political rights.

In January, the integration deal reached between the central government in Damascus and the SDF halted weeks of fighting. While some Kurdish politicians hail the integration as a door for the Kurds to participate in building the new Syria and to demand their rights through the constitution, others consider the step a result of pressure from Turkiye and the United States and potentially harmful for Kurdish interests.

articles.title: At halfway mark of third term, PM Modi to hold 'Chintan Shivir'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi on Wednesday directed setting up of over half a dozen groups comprising ministers, each having eight members, to brainstor.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi on Wednesday directed setting up of over half a dozen groups comprising ministers, each having eight members, to brainstorm on issues including self-improvement, communication and governance ahead of two-day “Chintan Shivir” of entire council of ministers scheduled next week, TOI has learnt.The retreat will be held at Seva Teerth and comes almost midway through the third term of Modi-led NDA govt. A similar Chintan Shivir was conducted on Oct 21, 2021, barely months after a major Cabinet reshuffle during the second term. At that time, deliberations focused on governance and policy making and this exercise was aimed at helping ministers better understand issues of governance. Different ministers had made detailed presentations with participation of their colleagues in the council.The next brainstorming session is expected to follow a similar format, with thematic discussions and presentations by different groups. This is being seen as taking stock of governance, improving coordination among ministries and preparing the govt’s future agenda.Officials said that recently ministries were asked to provide the actions taken on the recommendations of the 2021 Chintan Shivir meeting. Several directions were issued to ministers and ministries, including to have live dashboards of ministry’s activities, review progress and hold interactions with all staff to get feedback and ideas. “This was an indication that at any point of time there could be a review of progress across ministries,” said an official.Last week, the PM had asked all ministers to work on making official websites of ministries and departments more user-friendly.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Princess Diana’s brother claims Charles said she would be forgotten ‘soon enough’ just days after her death
articles.summary: The brother of the late Princess Diana, Charles Spencer, has claimed in his forthcoming memoir that King Charles told him days after her death that “we’ll forget her soon enough,” according to an extract published on Wednesday by the Daily Mail.
articles.body: The brother of the late Princess Diana, Charles Spencer, has claimed in his forthcoming memoir that King Charles told him days after her death that “we’ll forget her soon enough,” according to an extract published on Wednesday by the Daily Mail. Spencer claimed that Charles – then Prince of Wales – launched into a “stream of anger” over the phone after he argued that his sister would not have wanted William and Harry to take part in her funeral procession. The late Princess of Wales died in August 1997 after suffering internal injuries resulting from a high-speed car crash in Paris. Her sons, ages 15 and 12 at the time, walked in the funeral procession days later. Buckingham Palace pushed back against the claims by Spencer. In an unusually strong statement that attributed a reaction directly to the King, the palace suggested that Spencer’s judgment had been hampered by his grief. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” a palace spokesperson said in a statement. CNN has not seen the book, Swan Song, ahead of its publication, but a spokesperson for Penguin Random House confirmed to CNN that the passages quoted from the book are accurate. The Daily Mail obtained exclusive rights to publish excerpts as part of a series starting on Thursday, according to the paper, which has described the book as “explosive.” Spencer wrote about the tense phone call in his book, which publishes next week and is expected to include heavy criticism of the royal family. “Prince Charles continued his stream of anger, without me interrupting. Then he stopped,” Spencer wrote. “I assumed the pause signaled an effort to bring himself under control, but then he unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death.” “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’” Spencer wrote. “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: I don’t remember anything: Arizona man duct-taped to American Airlines seat for racist outburst speaks in court after flight diversion
articles.summary: US News: The Arizona man who was duct-taped to his seat and restrained with zip ties during an American Airlines flight told a Maryland court that he did not r.
articles.body: The Arizona man who was duct-taped to his seat and restrained with zip ties during an American Airlines flight told a Maryland court that he did not remember what happened during the mid-air disturbance that forced the plane to divert to Baltimore.Layne Lundeen, 67, appeared for his initial hearing in Annapolis on September 4, a day after American Airlines Flight 618 was diverted to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI).Lundeen faced charges of second-degree assault and disorderly conduct in connection with the incident. He was released on his own recognizance after a later bail review, and his next court appearance is scheduled for October 19.During his initial appearance, Lundeen said he remembered talking to the passenger sitting beside him but could not recall what happened afterward.The passenger was Jonathan Cahn, an author and Messianic rabbi. Cahn has said that a conversation between the two initially appeared friendly before Lundeen allegedly became increasingly agitated.According to police allegations, Lundeen became disruptive during the flight, which was travelling from Dallas-Fort Worth to Newark, New Jersey. Witnesses told investigators that he allegedly used profanities and racial slurs and became physically aggressive.Passengers and crew eventually restrained Lundeen using duct tape and zip ties, securing him to his seat for the remainder of the flight.The aircraft was then diverted to BWI, where Maryland Transportation Authority Police took Lundeen into custody.What happened on the plane?The incident unfolded on September 3 aboard American Airlines Flight 618.According to police accounts cited by The Baltimore Banner, Lundeen's behaviour became increasingly unruly during the flight. Witnesses alleged that he directed racial slurs at people on board and became physically aggressive.Former law enforcement officer Juan Mejia, who was among the passengers who intervened, told ABC News that he heard the disturbance and became involved as the situation escalated.Another passenger, Richard Olenick, also helped restrain Lundeen.The two men, together with flight attendants, eventually secured Lundeen with restraints until the plane landed in Baltimore.American Airlines confirmed that restraints are carried on its aircraft and can be used when necessary to maintain the safety and security of passengers and crew.Lundeen says he has no memory of the episodeAt his court appearance, Lundeen's account differed sharply from what witnesses described.He said he remembered speaking with Cahn but did not recall the alleged confrontation that followed. He also appeared confused about how he had ended up in Maryland rather than New Jersey.The court proceedings did not establish why Lundeen said he could not remember the incident.The allegations remain the subject of the criminal case, and Lundeen has not been convicted of the charges.The FBI is also gathering information about the incident.Flight continued after emergency landingAfter Lundeen was removed from the aircraft, Flight 618 continued to Newark.The incident has since drawn widespread attention after photographs showing Lundeen restrained with duct tape went viral online.Lundeen, who lives in Tucson, Arizona, has been identified as a former real-estate professional.
